“The language of the Republic is French” (article 2 of the Constitution).
csp-1-22: What is the place of the French language in the Republic?
French is the language of the Republic: of administration, school, justice and public services.
Regional languages are part of France's heritage (article 75-1).
csp-1-23: Which freedom lets everyone express their ideas?
Everyone may express ideas and opinions within the limits set by law (article 11 of the 1789 Declaration).
csp-1-25: What are the colours of the French flag?
Three vertical stripes: blue, white and red.
csp-1-26: Composed in 1792 by Rouget de Lisle.
csp-1-27: What is traditionally organised on the Champs-Élysées on 14 July?
Every 14 July the armed forces parade in Paris in front of the President of the Republic.
csp-1-28: The figure representing the French Republic.
A woman wearing the Phrygian cap, seen on stamps, coins and in town halls. A symbol, not a real person.
csp-1-30: “France is an indivisible, …, democratic and social Republic.” Complete article 1:
Article 1: “France is an indivisible, secular, democratic and social Republic.”
csp-1-34: Why must secularism be respected at school?
To protect pupils' freedom of conscience and keep state schools neutral.
Teachers are neutral and pupils may not wear conspicuous religious signs (2004 law).
csp-1-36: Can a child refuse to go to school for religious reasons?
No. Schooling is compulsory for all children aged 3 to 16, whatever their religion.
Religious beliefs do not allow refusing school or a compulsory subject.
csp-1-37: Does a person have the right not to believe in any religion?
Yes. Everyone is free to believe or not to believe.
Freedom of conscience allows having a religion, changing it or having none.
csp-2-1: The President appoints the Prime Minister (article 8), then the other ministers on his or her proposal.
csp-2-2: The National Assembly and the Senate.
Parliament passes laws and scrutinises the Government.
csp-2-3: What is executive power? The power:
To implement the laws and lead the country's policy.
It is held by the President of the Republic and the Government.
csp-2-4: Leaders are elected by citizens in:
In a democracy, power comes from the people, who choose their representatives in free elections.
csp-2-6: Everyone: people living in France, French or foreign, and the State itself.
Nobody is above the law, including politicians.
csp-2-7: What is the role of the judicial authority?
Delivering justice: settling disputes and punishing offences.
Under the Constitution, it is independent and protects individual liberty.
csp-2-8: What power does a judge hold?
The judge settles disputes and applies the penalties set by law.
csp-2-9: Judges are independent of political power.
csp-2-10: What happens if a minister breaks the law?
He or she can be prosecuted and tried, like anyone.
For acts in office, ministers are tried by the Court of Justice of the Republic; otherwise by ordinary courts.
csp-2-12: How many MPs sit in the National Assembly?
Elected by direct universal suffrage for 5 years.
csp-2-13: Every 3 years, for half of the seats.
Senators are elected for 6 years by indirect suffrage, by “grand electors” (mostly local officials).
csp-2-15: Who is elected in the presidential election?
Elected by direct universal suffrage for 5 years.
csp-2-16: From what age can you vote?
You must also be French and on the electoral roll. EU citizens can vote in municipal and European elections.
csp-2-17: For how long is the President elected?
Since 2002 (previously 7 years). No more than two consecutive terms.
csp-2-18: For how long are MPs elected?
The 577 MPs are elected by direct universal suffrage.
csp-2-19: For how long are senators elected?
Indirect suffrage; the Senate is renewed by half every 3 years.
csp-2-20: The President of the Republic and the Government.
The Government, led by the Prime Minister, decides and conducts the nation's policy.
csp-2-22: Who can vote in elections in France?
Adult French citizens on the electoral roll.
EU citizens living in France can also vote in municipal and European elections.
csp-2-23: All adult citizens can vote, whatever their sex, origin, religion or wealth.
Universal male suffrage dates from 1848; women have voted since 1944.
csp-2-24: About political parties, which statement is correct?
They are formed and operate freely.
Under article 4 of the Constitution they take part in elections and must respect democracy. Pluralism is guaranteed.
csp-2-25: What is the role of MPs?
Passing laws and scrutinising the Government.
They sit in the National Assembly and can bring down the Government with a motion of censure.
csp-2-29: Citizens, by direct universal suffrage, in the parliamentary elections.
Voters in each constituency elect their MP for 5 years.
csp-2-31: Who lives in the Élysée Palace?
The Élysée in Paris is the President's official residence and workplace.
csp-2-34: The mayor, with the municipal council.
csp-2-35: Does the President of the Republic have all the powers?
No. Powers are separated and the President must respect the Constitution.
Parliament passes laws and justice is independent. The President serves 5 years, at most two consecutive terms.
csp-2-36: The representative of the State in the département (and region).
Appointed by the President, the prefect ensures the law and public order are respected; prefectures issue residence permits.
csp-2-37: What is the role of Parliament?
Passing laws, scrutinising the Government and evaluating public policy.
Made up of the National Assembly and the Senate (article 24); it also votes the State budget.
csp-2-40: Which country is not an EU member?
For example Switzerland, Norway or the United Kingdom.
The EU has 27 member states. The UK left in 2020.
csp-2-41: Which condition is required to vote in European elections?
Being an EU citizen, adult and on the electoral roll.
In France, French citizens and EU citizens living in France can vote in European elections.
csp-2-42: How often are European elections held?
EU citizens elect the members of the European Parliament; the last election was in June 2024.
csp-2-44: What currency is used in France?
Euro coins and notes have circulated since 1 January 2002, replacing the franc.
csp-3-1: What is the name of France's current Constitution?
The Constitution of the Fifth Republic, of 4 October 1958.
The Republic's most important text; it has been amended several times.
csp-3-2: What is the text setting out the rights and duties of people living in France?
The 1789 Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen, part of the Constitution.
Its rights apply to everyone living in France. The 1946 preamble and the Environment Charter complete them.
csp-3-3: About individual rights, which statement is correct?
They are guaranteed by law but exercised with respect for others' rights and public order.
Liberty means being able to do anything that does not harm others (article 4 of the 1789 Declaration).
csp-3-4: What year does the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen date from?
Adopted on 26 August 1789, during the Revolution; it is part of today's Constitution.
csp-3-5: Which of these rights is a fundamental right?
For example freedom of expression, equality before the law or the right to security.
Fundamental rights are protected by the Constitution and by European and international texts.
csp-3-6: Which text guarantees rights and freedoms in France?
The Constitution, with the 1789 Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen.
The Constitutional Council checks that laws respect these rights.
csp-3-8: Which right allows a person to defend themselves in court?
The rights of the defence, including the right to a lawyer.
Everyone is entitled to a fair trial and presumed innocent until proven guilty. Legal aid can pay for a lawyer.
csp-3-10: Which text was adopted during the French Revolution?
The Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen (1789).
It proclaims that men are born and remain free and equal in rights.
csp-3-11: Which freedom allows a person to have no religion?
Guaranteed by secularism: believing, not believing or changing religion.
csp-3-12: A woman can have an abortion:
If she wishes, until the end of the 14th week of pregnancy.
Allowed since the 1975 Veil law; the freedom to have an abortion has been in the Constitution since 2024.
csp-3-13: Is it always possible to divorce?
Yes. Either spouse can ask for a divorce.
By mutual consent or through a judge, even if the other spouse disagrees.
csp-3-14: Abolished by the law of 9 October 1981 (Robert Badinter); its ban has been in the Constitution since 2007.
csp-3-15: About limits on individual freedoms, which statement is correct?
Freedoms can be limited by law, to protect public order or the rights of others.
For example, freedom of expression does not allow insults or calls to hatred.
csp-3-17: Yes. Reducing waste protects the environment.
Less waste means less pollution: sort, reuse and avoid unnecessary packaging.
csp-3-18: Throwing a bottle in the street is:
Forbidden and punished by a fine.
Littering is an offence; use bins and recycling containers.
csp-3-19: Why can individual freedoms be limited?
To protect public order, safety, public health and the rights of others.
Limits must be set by law and proportionate (e.g. highway code, smoking ban in public places).
csp-3-20: What should you do in case of an accident?
Protect, alert emergency services and, if possible, give first aid.
Emergency numbers: 15 (SAMU), 17 (police), 18 (fire brigade), 112 (European). Failing to help a person in danger is punished.
csp-3-21: Rights such as voting and standing for election, and duties such as respecting the law and taking part in defence.
Some public-sector jobs are reserved for French citizens.
csp-3-22: What does a person risk if they break the law?
A penalty: a fine, or even prison depending on the seriousness.
Offences are contraventions, délits and crimes; penalties are imposed by the courts.
csp-3-23: What is the role of the gendarmerie?
Ensuring safety and public order, mainly in rural and suburban areas.
A military force under the Interior Ministry that protects people and property and investigates.
csp-3-24: What is the role of the police?
Protecting people and property, maintaining public order and enforcing the law.
The national police mainly works in cities; in an emergency, call 17 or 112.
csp-3-25: An act forbidden by law and punished.
Three categories, from least to most serious: contravention, délit, crime.
csp-3-26: How can you reduce your waste?
By sorting, reusing and avoiding unnecessary packaging and waste.
E.g. buy loose products, repair, give away what you no longer use, compost food waste.
csp-3-27: Leaving a broken washing machine on the pavement is:
Forbidden: it is fly-tipping, punished by a fine.
Take broken appliances to a recycling centre or have the seller take them back.
csp-3-28: Exploiting a person, e.g. forcing them to work or into prostitution, after recruiting, moving or housing them.
A very serious offence. Victims can be protected and supported.
csp-3-29: What should a victim of violence do?
Call the police or gendarmerie (17 or 112) and file a complaint; she or he can get support.
For violence against women, 3919 is a free, anonymous helpline.
csp-4-2: A general who became Emperor of the French in 1804.
He created the Civil Code (1804), the lycées and the Legion of Honour.
csp-4-3: Which of these historical figures is French?
For example Joan of Arc, Napoleon I or General de Gaulle.
csp-4-4: Which Republic are we in today?
Founded in 1958 by General de Gaulle.
csp-4-10: In what year was the European Economic Community (EEC) created?
In 1957, by the Treaty of Rome.
Created by France, Germany, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg; it led to the EU.
csp-4-12: Who was the first President elected under the Fifth Republic?
csp-4-15: How many Republics has France had?
The Fifth Republic has existed since 1958.
csp-4-17: Its Constitution was approved by referendum on 28 September 1958.
csp-4-18: The national holiday, recalling the storming of the Bastille (1789) and the Fête de la Fédération (1790).
Symbols of the end of absolute monarchy and of national unity.
csp-4-19: Which war took place from 1914 to 1918?
It ended with the armistice of 11 November 1918; nearly 1.4 million French soldiers died.
csp-4-21: For example the Loire, the Seine, the Rhône or the Garonne.
The Loire is the longest; the Seine flows through Paris.
csp-4-22: For example Lyon, Marseille, Bordeaux or Toulouse.
Careful: Brussels (Belgium), Geneva (Switzerland) or Quebec (Canada) are French-speaking but not in France.
csp-4-23: Which ocean borders the west coast of France?
Mainland France is bordered by the Atlantic (west), the Channel, the North Sea and the Mediterranean (south).
csp-4-24: The largest city and seat of national institutions: Élysée, Government, Parliament.
csp-4-25: What is the capital of France?
Seat of the President, the Government and Parliament.
csp-4-26: On which continent is mainland France?
Mainland France is in Western Europe; France also has overseas territories on other continents and oceans.
csp-4-30: Which sea lies south of mainland France?
It borders the south coast and Corsica.
csp-4-31: Which city lies on the Mediterranean coast?
For example Marseille, Nice or Montpellier.
csp-4-32: A French island south-east of mainland France.
csp-4-40: A painter born in Russia who became French.
Known for colourful paintings and stained glass; he painted the ceiling of the Opéra Garnier.
csp-4-41: A music-hall artist born in the USA who became French and joined the Resistance.
An anti-racism campaigner, she entered the Panthéon in 2021.
csp-4-42: Who was a famous French female singer?
Famous for “La Vie en rose”; also Barbara or Dalida.
csp-4-43: A major museum in Paris, one of the most visited in the world.
A former royal palace; it houses the Mona Lisa.
csp-4-44: Who was Jean de La Fontaine?
A 17th-century French poet, famous for his Fables.
E.g. “The Crow and the Fox”, “The Grasshopper and the Ant”.
csp-4-45: For example Victor Hugo, Molière or Albert Camus.
Hugo wrote Les Misérables; Camus won the Nobel Prize in Literature.
csp-4-46: In which city is the Eiffel Tower?
Built by Gustave Eiffel for the 1889 World's Fair.
csp-4-47: A Christian holiday that is also a family celebration; a public holiday.
csp-5-2: Which emergency number calls the fire brigade?
112 is the European emergency number, valid throughout the EU.
csp-5-3: After getting your driving licence, what must you do to drive your car?
Insure it: car insurance is compulsory.
The registration certificate must also be up to date. Driving uninsured is an offence.
csp-5-4: Under what conditions is a marriage legally recognised?
It must be performed at the town hall by a registrar, with the free consent of both spouses, who are adults.
Only civil marriage is recognised; a religious one may only follow. Forced marriage and polygamy are forbidden.
csp-5-7: What must an employer do to set a salary?
Pay at least the SMIC and the minimums of the collective agreement.
Pay is set in the contract; equal work means equal pay for women and men.
csp-5-11: Who is helped by France Travail?
France Travail (formerly Pôle emploi) supports jobseekers, pays unemployment benefit and helps companies recruit.
csp-5-14: From what age can a minor work?
From 14, small holiday jobs are possible with parental consent and under conditions.
csp-5-16: A free number, available 24/7, to get help in danger or an emergency.
csp-5-17: About access to healthcare, which statement is correct?
Anyone living in France stably and legally is entitled to cover for health costs.
This is universal health protection (PUMa). Emergency care is always provided.
csp-5-18: For a non-urgent health problem, who should you see first?
Your GP (médecin traitant), or a pharmacist for advice.
Out of hours, call 116 117. Hospital emergencies are for serious situations.
csp-5-19: What is the role of the GP (médecin traitant)?
Following the patient's health, coordinating care and referring to specialists.
Declaring a GP to health insurance means better reimbursement.
csp-5-20: When should you go to hospital emergencies?
In a serious or life-threatening situation: serious injury, fainting, intense pain…
For a life-threatening emergency, call 15 or 112.
csp-5-21: What is the aim of compulsory vaccinations?
Protecting each person and the whole population against serious contagious diseases.
Eleven vaccines are compulsory for children born since 2018; required for nursery and school.
csp-5-25: To protect the child and ensure their education, health and safety.
Rights and duties exercised by both parents in the child's interest until adulthood; violence is forbidden.
csp-5-26: For all children aged 3 to 16 living in France, whatever their nationality.
Young people aged 16–18 must also be in training, apprenticeship, work or civic service.
csp-5-27: Which diploma do you get at the end of lycée?
It gives access to higher education.
csp-5-30: Must attend regularly (attendance obligation) and respect the school rules.
Absences must be justified by the parents.
cr-1-1: Which of these is a form of civic participation?
For example voting, volunteering in an association or taking part in your neighbourhood's life.
Civic participation means getting involved in collective and democratic life.
cr-1-3: What is a residence permit for?
Allowing a foreign national to stay legally in France.
Issued by the prefecture; depending on its type, it may also allow work.
cr-1-5: On which website can you find the symbol of the French Republic?
On official State websites, e.g. service-public.fr or “gouv.fr” sites.
The State logo combines Marianne, the tricolour flag and the motto.
cr-1-6: Complete the words of La Marseillaise: “Aux armes, citoyens...”
“… formez vos bataillons! Marchons, marchons!” (form your battalions, let us march)
cr-1-8: Under individual liberty, which is correct? A person can:
Freely choose their private life: religion, spouse, place to live or opinions, within the law.
Liberty means doing anything that does not harm others.
cr-1-9: About religious practice, which statement is correct?
Everyone can practise the religion of their choice, while respecting the law and public order.
Secularism guarantees free worship; the State recognises and funds no religion (1905 law).
cr-1-10: As a parent, can you refuse to let your child take part in mixed PE lessons?
No. PE lessons are compulsory and mixed for all pupils.
Religious beliefs do not allow refusing a school subject.
cr-1-12: Forbidden and without legal value in France.
Only a judge can grant a divorce. Equality of women and men also applies in marriage.
cr-1-15: What does the State do to fight discrimination?
It bans discrimination by law, punishes it and helps victims, notably through the Defender of Rights.
Discrimination in hiring or housing based on origin, sex or religion is punished.
cr-1-21: An employer refuses to hire women. What does the law say?
It is forbidden: it is discrimination punished by law.
Women and men must have the same chances and equal pay; victims can contact the Defender of Rights or the courts.
cr-1-31: In a state school, who may wear very visible religious signs?
The 2004 law bans conspicuous religious signs for pupils; teachers must remain neutral.
cr-1-35: Does secularism require public employees to be neutral towards users?
Yes. They must not show their religious beliefs at work.
They must treat all users equally, whatever their beliefs.
cr-1-39: What is forbidden by the school secularism charter?
Proselytism, refusing a lesson for religious reasons and, for pupils, conspicuous religious signs.
The charter (2013) reminds that school protects pupils from any pressure.
cr-2-2: The President has committed a crime. Which statement is correct?
During the term he or she cannot be prosecuted, but Parliament sitting as the High Court can remove them; afterwards they can be tried.
Articles 67 and 68 of the Constitution: nobody is above the law.
cr-2-3: The law is the expression of:
cr-2-6: Can a person vote in place of another?
No, voting is personal, except by proxy.
A proxy can be given online (maprocuration.gouv.fr), at the police station or gendarmerie.
cr-2-7: No. Voting is a right and a civic duty, but not compulsory in France.
Young French people are automatically registered at 18.
cr-2-8: At the end of the term, can the President decide to stay in power?
No. The President serves 5 years, at most two consecutive terms.
A new presidential election is then held.
cr-2-12: What is legislative power? The power:
It belongs to Parliament (National Assembly and Senate).
cr-2-13: Why separate the three powers in a democracy?
To prevent one person or institution from holding all power, and to protect freedoms.
Legislative passes laws, executive applies them, judicial judges (Montesquieu's idea).
cr-2-15: What is the role of the Government?
Deciding and conducting the nation's policy.
Led by the Prime Minister, it applies the laws and runs the administration (article 20).
cr-2-26: What is the Hôtel de Matignon?
The Prime Minister's residence and workplace, in Paris.
cr-2-31: How many regions are there in France?
Regions handle lycées, regional trains (TER) and economic development.
cr-2-34: What is the main role of the département?
Social welfare and solidarity (RSA, child welfare, elderly and disabled people), plus collèges and departmental roads.
France has 101 départements, 5 of them overseas.
cr-2-35: What is the main role of towns (communes)?
Running local services: civil registry, nursery and primary schools, planning, roads, canteens…
The mayor and council are elected for 6 years.
cr-2-36: About how many towns (communes) are there in France?
cr-3-1: Which freedom does assisted reproduction (PMA) refer to?
The freedom to have children and start a family.
Since the 2021 bioethics law, PMA is open to all women, in a couple or single.
cr-3-3: About the right to marry, which statement is correct?
Everyone is free to marry the person of their choice, if adult and consenting.
Forced marriage is forbidden; since 2013 marriage is open to same-sex couples.
cr-3-8: The organisation of public powers and fundamental rights and freedoms.
Its preamble refers to the 1789 Declaration, the 1946 preamble and the Environment Charter.
cr-3-10: What does the Environment Charter provide?
Everyone has the right to a healthy environment and the duty to help preserve it.
Adopted in 2004, part of the Constitution since 2005.
cr-3-11: Every human being must be respected and cannot be treated as an object.
It forbids torture, slavery or humiliating treatment.
cr-3-12: What does the right to demonstrate mean?
The right to gather in public to express opinions collectively.
A demonstration must be declared in advance to the town hall or prefecture and be peaceful.
cr-3-13: Medical techniques to help have a child; since 2021 open to female couples and single women.
cr-3-14: Which text is the hardest to amend?
A special procedure: vote by both chambers, then referendum or a three-fifths majority of Congress.
cr-3-17: The Republic's highest text: it organises the powers and guarantees rights and freedoms.
The current one is the Fifth Republic's, of 4 October 1958. All laws must respect it.
cr-3-18: Who can ask for an abortion?
Any pregnant woman who does not want to continue the pregnancy, adult or minor.
A minor can ask without parental consent, accompanied by an adult of her choice. Possible until the end of the 14th week.
cr-3-19: Does an adult French woman have the right to vote?
Yes. Women have had the right to vote in France since 1944.
They first voted in 1945 and have the same political rights as men.
cr-3-20: About social media, which statement is correct?
The law also applies online: harassment, insults or threats are punished.
Illegal content can be reported on PHAROS (internet-signalement.gouv.fr).
cr-3-21: Throwing a cigarette butt on the ground is:
Forbidden and punished by a fine.
Throwing any waste on the street is an offence.
cr-3-22: Can the State limit rights and freedoms?
Yes, but only by law and for specific reasons such as public order, safety or public health.
Limits must be necessary and proportionate; judges can review them.
cr-3-23: Which action shows respect for the environment?
For example sorting waste, saving water and energy or using public transport.
The Environment Charter says everyone must help preserve the environment.
cr-3-24: Which of these is an obligation?
For example respecting the law, paying taxes or sending your children to school.
Voting is a right and civic duty, but not a legal obligation.
cr-3-26: Why should you sort your waste?
To recycle materials, reduce pollution and preserve natural resources.
Sorting rules are set by your town.
cr-3-28: What should you do when police or gendarmes give orders?
Comply; you can contest afterwards through legal channels.
Refusing to comply, e.g. at a traffic check, is an offence.
cr-3-30: What is an example of assisting a person in danger?
Calling emergency services (15, 18 or 112) for an injured or unwell person, and helping if it is safe.
Failure to assist a person in danger is punished (article 223-6 of the Criminal Code).
cr-3-31: Which example shows a limit on freedom to protect the general interest?
For example compulsory seat belts or the smoking ban in public places.
These rules limit individual freedom to protect everyone's health and safety.
cr-3-32: What should you do if you witness violence?
Alert the police or gendarmerie (17 or 112) and help the victim without endangering yourself.
Failing to act when you safely could is punished. For violence against women, 3919 listens and advises.
cr-3-34: Which obligation applies to everyone living in France, whatever their nationality?
Everyone must also, for example, declare income and send their children to school.
cr-3-35: Which is an example of a crime?
Crimes are the most serious offences, tried by the assize court or departmental criminal court.
cr-3-36: Which is an example of a délit (offence)?
For example theft or driving without a licence.
Délits are tried by the criminal court; punished by fines and sometimes prison.
cr-3-37: The police and gendarmerie, under the State's authority.
They protect people and property and enforce the law.
cr-3-38: About waste, which statement is correct?
It must be sorted and put in the right places: bins, recycling containers, recycling centres.
Fly-tipping and littering are punished by fines.
cr-4-1: He reigned from 1643 to 1715 and built the Palace of Versailles.
cr-4-6: Why is the Shoah studied at school?
To pass on the memory of the genocide of the Jews and fight racism and antisemitism.
About 6 million European Jews were murdered by the Nazis, including nearly 76,000 deported from France.
cr-4-10: Under which president was the death penalty abolished?
The abolition law was carried by Justice Minister Robert Badinter.
cr-4-11: Which political system was set up during the Revolution in 1792?
Proclaimed in September 1792, after the fall of the monarchy.
cr-4-15: Abolished by the law of 9 October 1981.
cr-4-17: In what year did the First World War start?
It lasted from 1914 to 1918 and ended with the armistice of 11 November 1918.
cr-4-18: Where did the 1944 landings take place?
They opened the way to the liberation of France; another landing took place in Provence in August 1944.
cr-4-19: Which continent was most affected by French decolonisation after 1945?
Many African countries became independent around 1960; Algeria in 1962.
cr-4-22: Which country shares a land border with mainland France?
For example Belgium, Luxembourg, Germany, Switzerland, Italy, Spain, Andorra or Monaco.
Mainland France has land borders with these eight countries.
cr-4-31: Which country borders mainland France to the north-east?
Germany (as well as Belgium and Luxembourg).
To the east also Switzerland; to the south-east, Italy.
cr-4-32: Where are France's main economic activities?
Mostly in large cities and their surroundings, especially the Paris region.
Île-de-France produces about 30% of the country's wealth; Lyon, Marseille and Toulouse are also major centres.
cr-4-33: Which of these countries attracts the most visitors each year?
The most visited country in the world, with about 100 million international tourists a year.
cr-4-34: Where do most French people live?
In towns and cities: about 80% of the population.
Large urban areas (Paris, Lyon, Marseille…) are home to much of the population.
cr-4-35: Which region has the largest population?
Over 12 million inhabitants, almost one French person in five.
cr-4-37: Which French département is the most touristic?
Tens of millions of visitors a year; Seine-et-Marne, with Disneyland Paris, is also very visited.
cr-4-39: How many people speak French in the world?
According to the 2026 report of the International Organisation of La Francophonie: 396 million, many in Africa.
cr-4-44: How does French rank among the world's most spoken languages?
According to the OIF report published in 2026, French is 4th, after English, Mandarin and Spanish; it was 5th in the previous report.
cr-4-45: Which famous cathedral was partly destroyed by fire in 2019?
Hit by fire on 15 April 2019, it reopened in December 2024 after restoration.
cr-4-46: Who was a famous French woman writer?
For example George Sand, Colette, Simone de Beauvoir or Marguerite Yourcenar.
Yourcenar was the first woman elected to the Académie française, in 1980.
cr-4-49: For example the national holiday on 14 July or the Fête de la musique on 21 June.
The Fête de la musique was created in France in 1982.
cr-5-6: What is one condition to take the driving test?
Being at least 17 for the B licence (car).
You must also pass the highway code test then the driving test; learning can start at 15 with supervised driving.
cr-5-7: A rental lease is valid if it is:
Written and signed by the tenant and the landlord.
It states the rent, duration and deposit; an inventory is made on arrival and departure.
cr-5-17: When an employer wants an employee to work longer than the contract says:
These are overtime hours: they must be paid more or compensated with rest.
In principle +25% for the first 8 overtime hours of the week, then +50%, unless a collective agreement says otherwise.
cr-5-18: Supporting jobseekers, paying their benefits and helping companies recruit.
France Travail replaced Pôle emploi in 2024; you can register online.
cr-5-19: In a company, the right to join a union allows:
Employees to create or join a union to defend their interests.
Union freedom is guaranteed by the Constitution; no employee can be penalised for being a member.
cr-5-21: What are the conditions for unemployment benefit?
Having lost your job involuntarily, having worked enough before, being registered with France Travail and actively looking for work.
Generally at least 6 months (130 days) of work in the last 24 months; resigning usually gives no right, with exceptions.
cr-5-22: Schooling is compulsory from age 3 since 2019; public nursery school is free.
cr-5-23: What is the diploma taken at the end of collège called?
Taken at the end of year 3e.
cr-5-24: Pupils' parents have the right to:
For example be informed of their child's results, meet the teachers and elect representatives.
Parents are members of the school community.
cr-5-25: Who can eat at the school canteen?
All schoolchildren, without discrimination, when the town offers the service.
Since 2017 the law makes canteen enrolment in primary schools a right for every pupil; prices often depend on family income.
cr-5-28: At school, parents are forbidden to:
For example disrupt the school, proselytise or stop their child from attending a compulsory lesson.
Parents must respect the school rules, the teachers and secularism.
cr-5-31: When are the Christmas school holidays?
Two weeks, at the end of December and the start of January.
Dates are set by the Ministry of Education and are the same throughout mainland France.
cr-5-32: At school, a child with a disability:
Has the right to attend school, with the necessary adjustments.
School is inclusive: the child can be helped, e.g. by an AESH support assistant.

s1-1: At work, a woman becomes team leader. A colleague refuses to follow her instructions because she is a woman.
He must respect her authority: women and men are equal.
Equality between women and men is a principle of the Republic. A woman can lead a team just like a man.
s1-2: A landlord refuses to rent his flat to a family because they are Muslim.
It is forbidden discrimination, punished by law.
Refusing housing because of religion, origin or sex is punished. The victim can contact the Defender of Rights or file a complaint.
s1-3: A restaurant refuses to serve a wheelchair user, with no safety reason.
No, refusing a service because of a disability is discrimination.
Disability is one of the forbidden grounds of discrimination.
s1-4: Your 19-year-old friend's family is arranging her marriage to a man she does not want to marry.
Forced marriage is forbidden: both spouses must freely consent.
A person threatened with forced marriage can get help, e.g. by calling 3919, and be protected.
s1-5: In a meeting, a colleague makes racist remarks about someone.
Report it: racist insults are punished by law.
Freedom of expression does not allow insults or hate speech. You can alert the employer, the Defender of Rights or file a complaint.
s1-6: At the town hall, the employee serving you wears a very visible religious sign.
A public employee must remain neutral and not show religious beliefs.
Neutrality applies to public employees, not to users.
s1-7: You go to the town hall wearing a visible religious sign.
Yes, users of public services may wear a religious sign.
Only the face must remain uncovered in public spaces.
s1-8: In the street, a person wears clothing that covers their whole face.
It is forbidden to hide your face in public spaces.
Since a 2010 law, covering the face in public spaces is forbidden, with exceptions such as health reasons.
s1-9: Your friend wants to leave his religion. His family threatens him.
He is free to change or leave his religion; threats are punished.
Freedom of conscience allows believing, not believing or changing religion.
s1-10: In a job interview, a candidate is asked whether she plans to have children.
This question should not be asked: a job cannot be refused for this reason.
Refusing to hire a woman because she is pregnant or wants children is forbidden discrimination.
s1-11: In a job interview, the recruiter asks about your religion.
Religion must play no part in choosing a candidate.
Religious beliefs are a forbidden ground of discrimination in hiring.
s1-12: Before an election, your neighbour tells you who to vote for and wants to check your ballot.
The vote is free and secret: nobody can impose your choice.
You vote alone in the booth. Pressuring a voter is punished.
s1-13: A friend says the rules of his religion are above the laws of the Republic.
The laws of the Republic apply to everyone, whatever their beliefs.
Secularism guarantees freedom of belief, but nobody can use religion to avoid the common law.
s1-14: A shopkeeper puts up a sign: “No foreigners”.
It is forbidden discrimination, punished by law.
Refusing entry because of origin or nationality is punished by the Criminal Code.
s1-15: A married woman wants to open a bank account in her own name, without her husband's consent.
Yes, she does not need her husband's consent.
Since 1965, a married woman can open an account and work without her husband's permission.
s1-16: You want to publish online a text criticising a Government decision.
Yes, as long as you insult no one and do not call for hatred or violence.
Freedom of expression allows criticising politicians, within the limits set by law.
s1-17: Two men want to get married at the town hall.
Yes, marriage has been open to same-sex couples since 2013.
s1-18: A parent wants to withdraw his daughter from mixed swimming lessons at school.
Swimming lessons are part of compulsory teaching.
Compulsory lessons, including sport and swimming, apply to all pupils; religious beliefs do not allow refusing them.
s1-19: A friend wants his 15-year-old daughter to get married.
It is forbidden: you must be at least 18 to marry.
The minimum age to marry in France is 18, for women and men.
s1-20: In a state school, a teacher promotes his religion during class.
No, the teacher must remain neutral.
State schools are secular; teachers must neither show nor promote their religious beliefs.
s1-21: A pupil at a state collège wants to come to class wearing a conspicuous religious sign.
It is forbidden in state schools, collèges and lycées.
The law of 15 March 2004; dialogue comes before any sanction.
s1-22: Your town is thinking of paying for a new place of worship.
In principle, the State and towns fund no religion.
The Republic recognises, pays and subsidises no religion; special rules apply in Alsace-Moselle.
s1-23: At an official ceremony, La Marseillaise is played.
Stand up and stay silent, out of respect.
La Marseillaise is the national anthem.
s1-24: During a heatwave, your elderly neighbour lives alone and rarely goes out.
Checking on her and telling the town hall if she needs help.
Town halls keep a register of vulnerable people to help them during heatwaves.
s1-25: You discover that a female colleague is paid less than a man for the same job.
Equal work means equal pay for women and men.
Equal pay is a legal obligation for all employers.
s1-26: A local newspaper publishes an article criticising your town's mayor.
Yes, press freedom allows it, within the law.
The press may criticise public officials but not defame or insult them.
s1-27: A company systematically rejects candidates whose names sound foreign.
It is hiring discrimination, punished by law.
Origin, real or assumed, and names are forbidden grounds of discrimination.
s1-28: At work, a colleague is regularly insulted and excluded because he is gay.
It is forbidden: sexual orientation is protected against discrimination and harassment.
The employer must protect staff; the victim can contact the Defender of Rights or file a complaint.
s2-1: You receive a fine notice for an offence you did not commit.
Contest it, following the procedure on the notice.
A fine can be contested within the time limit and procedure indicated, e.g. online.
s2-2: You disagree with a town hall decision about you.
Ask the town hall to review it, then go to the administrative court if needed.
Administrative decisions can be challenged: first with the administration, then before an administrative judge.
s2-3: On election day, you will be away and cannot vote.
Give a proxy to another voter.
Proxies can be given online (maprocuration.gouv.fr), at a police station or gendarmerie.
s2-4: A candidate offers you money in exchange for your vote.
It is forbidden: buying or selling votes is punished.
Gifts or promises to obtain votes are electoral offences.
s2-5: You have an idea to improve life in your neighbourhood.
Propose it to the town hall, the neighbourhood council or at a public meeting.
Citizens can take part in local life: meetings, councils, petitions, associations.
s2-6: Your Moroccan friend has lived in France for 15 years and wants to vote in municipal elections.
No: only French and EU citizens can vote in municipal elections.
Municipal voting rights are reserved to French citizens and to EU citizens on the rolls.
s2-7: Your Spanish neighbour lives in France and wants to vote in municipal elections.
Yes, if she is on the supplementary electoral rolls.
EU citizens living in France can vote in municipal and European elections.
s2-8: A law seems unfair to you.
Respect it and act democratically to change it.
In a democracy you can criticise, protest, petition or lobby your representatives, but must respect the law in force.
s2-9: The prefect issues an order banning fires in the département's forests in summer.
Respect the order: it is binding.
Prefectural orders apply to everyone; they can be challenged before the administrative court.
s2-10: You want to track your residence permit application.
On the official ANEF website (digital administration for foreigners in France).
Most applications are made and tracked online on ANEF. Paying sites promising faster procedures are not official.
s2-11: At your wedding at the town hall, the mayor performs the ceremony.
As a registrar (officier d'état civil), representing the State.
The mayor is both the town's elected leader and the State's agent for civil records.
s2-12: A police officer asks to see your papers in the street.
Show an identity document or your residence permit.
Identity checks are provided by law; a foreign national must be able to show the documents allowing their stay.
s2-13: Your neighbour, a French citizen, is summoned to be a juror at the assize court.
Attend: it is a civic duty, unless a serious reason is accepted.
Failing to respond without a legitimate reason can mean a fine.
s2-14: The President wants to change the Constitution alone.
No: an amendment must be voted by Parliament, then approved by referendum or by Congress.
Article 89 sets a demanding amendment procedure.
s2-15: Your son, a French citizen, has just turned 16.
Register for the citizen census at the town hall (or online).
Compulsory within 3 months after turning 16; it leads to the defence and citizenship day and automatic voter registration.
s2-16: On voting day, a friend offers to vote in your place with your voter card.
No, it is electoral fraud; only proxies are allowed.
Voting is personal; voting for someone else without a proxy is punished.
s2-17: You are looking for reliable information about your rights and procedures.
Which official website can you use?
The official French administration website for individuals.
s2-18: You have a small dispute with a neighbour (a damaged fence).
Go to a free court conciliator (conciliateur de justice).
The conciliator helps reach an amicable agreement; for many small disputes this step is required before court.
s2-19: You think an administration treated you unfairly and in a discriminatory way.
Whom can you contact for free?
The Defender of Rights (Défenseur des droits).
An independent authority defending people against administrations and discrimination.
s2-20: You want to raise a neighbourhood problem with your MP.
Write to your MP, the representative of your constituency, or meet them at their surgery.
MPs' contact details are on the National Assembly website.
s3-1: In the street, you find a wallet with money and an identity card.
Take it to the police, gendarmerie or lost-property office.
Keeping found property without trying to return it can be punished.
s3-2: You have a car accident with no injuries with another driver.
Fill in a joint accident report (constat amiable) together and inform your insurer.
If anyone is injured, call emergency services first (15, 18 or 112).
s3-3: Your neighbour makes a lot of noise almost every night after 10 pm.
Talk to him calmly, then use a conciliator or the police if it continues.
Night-time noise is an offence; dialogue comes first.
s3-4: A friend tells you her husband hits her.
Call 17 if in danger, 3919 to be listened to, and file a complaint.
Domestic violence is a serious offence; courts can order protection measures.
s3-5: You think a child in your building is being mistreated.
Free, 24/7. In immediate danger, call 17 or 112.
s3-6: A person collapses in front of you in a shop.
Call emergency services (15 or 112) and stay with them, following instructions.
Failing to help a person in danger is punished.
s3-7: Someone insults and threatens you on social media.
Keep screenshots, report the messages and file a complaint.
Online insults and threats are punished; report content on PHAROS.
s3-8: A teenager shares an intimate photo of a classmate without consent.
It is a serious offence, even between minors.
Sharing intimate images without consent is punished. Victims of harassment can call 3018.
s3-9: You receive a message seemingly from your benefits office asking for your bank details.
Do not reply or click: it is probably a scam to report.
Administrations never ask for bank codes by message. Help: cybermalveillance.gouv.fr.
s3-10: You worked a few months this year on a small salary.
Yes, the income declaration is compulsory even if you pay no tax.
Everyone living in France must declare income every year; it also gives access to some benefits.
s3-11: You have expired medicines at home.
What should you do with them?
Take them back to the pharmacy.
Pharmacies collect unused medicines free of charge.
s3-12: At a collection point, e.g. in a shop or recycling centre.
Shops selling batteries must take them back free of charge.
s3-13: In a bar, a customer lights a cigarette indoors.
No, smoking is forbidden in enclosed public places.
s3-14: In the car, you want to reply to a message while driving.
It is forbidden: stop in an authorised place.
Holding your phone while driving means a fine and loss of points.
s3-15: After a meal with several alcoholic drinks, you must go home.
Do not drive: take a taxi, public transport or let a sober person drive.
Drink-driving is a major cause of accidents and an offence.
s3-16: You need to go shopping and think of leaving your 4-year-old alone at home.
A young child must not be left unsupervised: it is dangerous and can be punished.
Parents must ensure their child's safety.
s3-17: A parent thinks a slap is a good way to raise a child.
Physical punishment, even light, is forbidden.
Since 2019 the law states that parental authority is exercised without physical or psychological violence.
s3-18: You want to file a complaint, but at the police station you are told to come back another day.
The police and gendarmerie must take complaints.
Any victim can file a complaint, whatever their nationality.
s3-19: Your neighbour regularly hits his dog and leaves it without food.
Animal cruelty is punished; you can report it.
You can alert the police, gendarmerie or an animal protection association.
s3-20: A person is held in police custody (garde à vue).
To have a lawyer and to have a relative informed.
Also a doctor and an interpreter if needed.
s3-21: At a court hearing, you do not understand French well.
Anyone prosecuted who does not understand French is entitled to an interpreter.
s3-22: You need a lawyer but your income is very low.
Legal aid (aide juridictionnelle), covering all or part of the lawyer's fees.
Granted according to income; apply at the court or online.
s3-23: Your landlord enters your flat while you are away, without your consent.
No: the rented flat is your home; he needs your consent.
s3-24: At work, a manager makes repeated sexual remarks to an employee.
It is sexual harassment, forbidden and punished; the employer must act.
The victim can alert the employer, labour inspectorate, Defender of Rights or file a complaint.
s3-25: A 15-year-old wants to buy alcohol in a shop.
Refuse: selling alcohol to minors is forbidden.
The seller can ask for ID.
s3-26: You see a pile of waste dumped by the roadside.
Report it to the town hall.
s3-27: A family plans to have their daughter undergo FGM during holidays abroad.
It is a crime under French law, even if committed abroad.
Anyone worried about a girl can call 119; courts can prevent her from leaving the country.
s4-1: On 11 November, your town holds a ceremony at the war memorial.
The 1918 armistice and those who died in the First World War.
A public holiday also honouring all who died for France.
s4-2: In September, your town announces the European Heritage Days.
Days when many monuments can be visited, often for free.
Places usually closed to the public open their doors.
s4-3: Your child's school organises a visit to the Shoah Memorial.
To pass on the memory of the genocide of the Jews and fight racism.
The duty of remembrance helps young people understand where racism and antisemitism lead.
s4-4: 8 May is a public holiday and flags are put up in your town.
The Allied victory and the end of the Second World War in Europe (1945).
s4-5: Your 20-year-old daughter, living in France, wants to visit a national museum like the Louvre.
Nothing: national museums are free for under-26s living in the EU.
s4-6: On 21 June, musicians play in every street of your town.
s4-7: On the evening of 14 July, your town holds a dance and fireworks.
It recalls the storming of the Bastille (1789) and the Fête de la Fédération (1790).
s4-8: You visit the Panthéon in Paris.
People who marked French history, such as Victor Hugo, Marie Curie or Joséphine Baker.
s4-9: During a visit, a friend wants to carve his name on a historic monument.
It is damage, punished by law.
Heritage belongs to everyone and must be protected.
s4-10: Your neighbour speaks Breton with his family.
Yes: regional languages are part of France's heritage.
French is the language of the Republic, but everyone may speak other languages (article 75-1).
s4-11: Your child's class visits a cathedral to study its architecture.
Yes: it is a cultural and historical visit, not religious teaching.
Secular schools can teach about religious heritage.
s4-12: You go on holiday in the Alps.
What is the highest summit in France?
Over 4,800 metres, on the border with Italy.
s5-1: You sign the lease for your first rented flat.
Which insurance must you take out?
The tenant must be insured at least against rental risks (fire, water damage) and give the certificate to the landlord.
s5-2: For an unfurnished flat, the landlord asks for three months' rent as a deposit.
For an unfurnished flat, the deposit is limited to one month's rent excluding charges.
For a furnished flat, two months.
s5-3: In January, your landlord wants to evict you.
The winter truce: in principle no evictions from 1 November to 31 March.
An eviction always requires a court decision.
s5-4: You leave your flat in good condition. The landlord does not return your deposit.
It must be returned within one month if the exit inventory matches.
Two months if there are differences; disputes can go to the departmental conciliation commission.
s5-5: In the evening, your child has a fever but does not seem seriously ill. The surgery is closed.
Call 116 117 to reach a duty doctor.
If 116 117 is not yet available in your area, call 15. For life-threatening emergencies, call 15.
s5-6: Someone suddenly feels strong chest pain.
Strong chest pain can be a life-threatening emergency.
s5-7: You have lost your Carte Vitale.
Request a new one, e.g. from your ameli online account.
Health insurance replaces it free of charge.
s5-8: You do not have a GP (médecin traitant) yet.
To be followed and better reimbursed by health insurance.
Without a declared GP, consultations are in principle less well reimbursed.
s5-9: Your employer offers group complementary health insurance (mutuelle).
The employer must offer it and pay at least half.
Since 2016 private employers must offer it and fund at least 50% of the contribution.
s5-10: You want to enrol your baby in a nursery.
The child must have had the compulsory vaccinations.
Eleven vaccines are compulsory for children born since 1 January 2018.
s5-11: You have just lost your job.
Registration gives support in finding work and, under conditions, benefits.
s5-12: An employer offers you work without a contract or payslip.
It deprives the employee of health, pension and unemployment rights.
s5-13: You get injured at your workplace.
The employer then declares the work accident; related care is covered.
s5-14: You have worked full time for a year.
How much paid leave do you have?
s5-15: Your hourly wage is below the SMIC.
It is forbidden: pay cannot be below the SMIC.
Collective agreements may set higher minimums.
s5-16: Your employer has not paid your salary for two months.
Claim it in writing, then go to the industrial tribunal (prud'hommes) if needed.
The labour inspectorate can also advise.
s5-17: Enrol them in école maternelle: schooling is compulsory from age 3.
Enrolment in a state school is done at the town hall, then at the school.
s5-18: Your child is ill and cannot go to school.
Inform the school and justify the absence.
s5-19: Your child has just arrived in France and does not speak French yet.
A place in an ordinary class with support to learn French.
Pupils new to French get extra French teaching.
s5-20: Your 16-year-old son wants to stop school and stay home.
From 16 to 18 he must be in training, apprenticeship, work or civic service.
The training obligation has applied up to 18 since 2020.
s5-21: Your baby has just been born.
Declare the birth at the town hall within five days.
Often done directly from the maternity ward.
s5-22: Give your new address to the administrations (tax, CAF, health insurance…).
A service-public.fr online service lets you notify several bodies at once.
s5-23: Your rent is high and your income low.
Which body can pay a housing benefit?
Housing aid depends on income, rent and family situation; apply online.
s5-24: You want to get rid of an old sofa.
Take it to the recycling centre or use the town's bulky-waste collection.
Abandoned bulky waste is fly-tipping, fined.
s5-25: You change address and you have a car.
Update the address on your registration certificate within a month, on the ANTS website.
s5-26: You have a driving licence from a non-EU country and live in France.
Depending on the country, you must exchange it for a French licence, usually within a year of your first residence permit.
Apply online on ANTS; not all countries allow an exchange.
s5-27: It is your first year declaring income in France.
Make the declaration, online on impots.gouv.fr or on paper for a first declaration.
s5-28: Several banks refuse to open an account for you.
The right to an account: the Banque de France can designate a bank that must open one.
Everyone living in France is entitled to a basic bank account.
s5-29: You are having a party at home on Saturday night.
Your neighbours' peace: night-time noise is forbidden.
Warning neighbours is polite but does not allow excessive noise.
s5-30: You want to improve your French.
Take the courses offered with the republican integration contract (CIR) or by associations, often free.
The CIR can include free language training.
s5-31: An ad promises you a job if you first pay registration fees.
Do not pay: an employer has no reason to make you pay for a job.
Often a scam; report it on internet-signalement.gouv.fr.
s5-32: You need medicine on a Sunday.
To the duty pharmacy (pharmacie de garde).
Its address is posted on pharmacies or online.
